articles.title: Identification ofSpecies Native to South Korea Using Molecular and Morphological Characteristics
articles.full_text:
Introduction

The genusL. belongs to the Fabaceae (Leguminosae) family and is the third largest family of flowering plants worldwide. Approximately 150–210 species are distributed across Europe, Asia, and North America, and the majority of species is found in the Mediterranean (;). To date, approximately 17–21species have been reported in Korea (;;).L. belongs to the Fabeae (syn. Vicieae) tribe along withL.,Mill.,L., andFed. (). Furthermore, thegenus is divided into two subgenera,L. (22 sections) andPeterm. [=(SCHUR) ROUY, five sections], based on the presence of stipule nectaries, relative peduncle length, subtending leaves, and number of flowers per inflorescence (;).

Many Fabaceae species are economically important as crops used in food, herbal medicine, petroleum materials, and animal feeds (). The genushas the advantage of primarily containing dual-purpose crops (). Representativespecies in agriculture areRoth andL., which have been used as green manure, cover, and forage crops. The ecological role ofspecies such asandL. as hosts to nitrogen-fixing bacteria () has the ability to fix free nitrogen from the air (). It helps to fertilize the soil by the fixed nitrogen released and making it available to other plants in agricultural and natural systems. In South Korea,species are distributed in various habitats. For example,(L.) Schreb. and(L.) Gray is widely distributed in range of grasslands, fields, cultivated areas, hill slopes, and roadsides, andA. Braun,Y.N.Lee,Fisch. & C.A.Mey., andMatsum are mainly distributed in forests, mountain, and hill areas.var.H. Lév.,Nakai, andOhwi are known as endemic plants of Korea, which have a restricted distribution with more threat to extinction than any other widely distributed species (). Hence, there is an urgency of protecting the species to conserve the biological diversity. Recently, the agricultural utility and ecological roles ofspecies have been recognized, and many studies on the genus are actively underway (,;;;).

Several candidate DNA regions in plastids, including,, andspacers have been recommended for use in plant species identification (;). Theandgenes are well conserved in the plastid coding region of most plant species. They are most promising coding regions in chloroplasts for plant species identification, with low transition and transversion rates. Similarly, due to the high level of sequence divergence,spacers region has been considered as the best candidate plant barcode (). However, species discrimination has previously been impossible when using single DNA barcodes for species identification. Hence, the Consortium for the Barcode of Life Plant Working Group suggested seven candidate plastid DNA regions (spacer,gene,gene,gene,gene,spacer, andspacer) and recommended the two-locus combination of+as a standard plant barcode (;). In addition, combining nuclear [internal transcribed spacer (ITS)] and plastid (,, and) regions has been recognized as a potential method of classifying various plant species (;;). In eukaryotes, the ITS region is present in the nuclear 45S ribosomal RNA (rDNA) genes, which can be further divided into the ITS1 and ITS2 regions. It has been proven to be the most suitable area for DNA barcoding, as it has a high efficiency of PCR amplification (93.8%) in most plant species (). The use of multiple DNA barcodes may provide sufficient identification power for closely related species ().

Similarly, morphological markers have been studied in combination with molecular markers as an efficient method of species classification (;;). Morphological data always play a key role in plant species classification based on phylogeny (). However, morphological studies require in-depth knowledge of characteristics or the number of species. Molecular tools using DNA barcodes for taxonomic identification, species delimitation, and access to phylogeny have the potential to overcome these difficulties faced by taxonomists (). However, it is very difficult to resolve recently diverged species or new species generated through hybridization if there is no universal sequence of common region as DNA barcode, and sufficient sequence divergence preserved in the domains of all living organisms is necessary for species classification (). DNA barcoding can be used together with traditional morphology, and it is necessary to use data derived from morphology in tandem with DNA sequence data (;;). Thus, integrating DNA sequencing, morphology, and ecology would lead to successful species classification ().

Morphological and DNA barcoding studies have been carried out to discriminate amongspecies. In terms of morphology, style shape, stipule margin, and size, tendril, leaflets, flower length, peduncles, presence/absence of stipule nectaries, calyx teeth, hairs, legume shape, and ovary characteristics are known to be important for species identification (;). Karyological studies using chromosomes, pollen morphology, characters, and testa texture of seeds have also been carried out in, and these traits have been recognized as important taxonomic keys (;;;). However, most of these taxonomic traits require specialized taxonomic knowledge and experience, and vast quantities of morphological information are required at each plant growth stage.

The ITS region of the nuclear genome was initially recommended for use in identifyingspecies (;;). Furthermore, the efficiency of species identification has been evaluated using different plastid barcode regions (), and 161species have been identified using a combination of barcoding loci such as,,,, ITS1, and ITS2 (). Relationships analysis within thegenus has revealed 10 sections, including one composed of East Asian species found in Korea, using molecular and stylar features to create the phylogeny (). However, only the ITS region has been used in barcoding, and there has been no research into the morphological features of the 19taxa distributed in South Korea. Therefore, the aim of the present study was to confirm the suitability of various barcoding (ITS2,, and) regions together with morphological traits for the identification of Koreanspecies.

Materials and Methods

Plant Materials and DNA Extraction

Samples of 19taxa were collected from 59 different locations in South Korea (and). Voucher specimens were deposited to the Herbarium Conservation Center of the National Institute of Agricultural Sciences (). Barcode sequence of ITS2,, andfor 33species (about 88 accessions) conserved at the National Agrobiodiversity Center, South Korea were downloaded from NCBI GenBank. These data were combined with the present study to increase the efficient conservation and utilization ofaccessions in South Korea (). Genomic DNA (gDNA) was extracted using DNeasyPlant Mini kits (Qiagen, Hilden, Germany) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Freeze-dried leaves were used for DNA extraction and were ground into a powder. DNA was resuspended in 100 ml water, and dilutions were made up to 10 ng μl, after which samples were stored at −20°C. DNA quality and quantity were measured using 1% (w/v) agarose gel and a spectrophotometer (Epoch, BioTek, Winooski, VT, United States).

Polymerase Chain Reaction Amplification and Sequencing

The sequences of the universal primers for ITS2,,, and general PCR reaction conditions were obtained from previous studies (;). Amplification reactions were carried out in a total volume of 20 μl containing 10× PCR buffer, 0.1 mM primers, 0.2 mM each deoxyribonucleotide triphosphate (dNTP), 1 U Taq DNA polymerase (Inclone, South Korea), and 200 ng template DNA. High-quality PCR products were sequenced from both directions by Macrogen, South Korea to reduce sequencing error. All sequences were submitted to the National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI;).

Data Analysis and Phylogenetic Analysis Based on Barcoding Regions

Consensus sequences of barcoding regions (ITS2,, and) were manually edited using the BioEdit program (ver.7.0.9, Tom Hall Ibis Biosciences, United States). Sequences were aligned using the “ClustalW” package in MEGA version X () and were evaluated for nucleotide variation, number of segregating sites, and informative sites. Nucleotide diversity (π) analysis and Tajima’s test (D) were conducted in DnaSP version 5.10.01 (). To assess individual-level discrimination rates for each single marker and all possible combinations, “Best Match” and “Best Close Match” analysis was carried out in the TAXONDNA software package (). For phylogenetic analysis, maximum likelihood trees were obtained using IQ-TREE version 1.6.2 software (). In IQ-TREE, the Best Fit Substitution Model option was selected based on the Bayesian information criterion. Model tests were conducted for each region, and Best Fit Substitution Models were obtained for ITS2 (K2P + I),(GTR + F),(JC + I), ITS2 +(TIM + G4),+(TVM + G4), ITS2 +(TNE + I), and++(TIM + G). Maximum likelihood trees were tested with bootstrap analysis adjusted to 1000 nonparametric bootstrap replicates in whichL. was used as outgroup. Species discrimination was considered successful only when all conspecific individuals generated a monophyletic clade, and species identification was evaluated using bootstrap values ().

Phylogenetic Analysis Based on Morphological Data

A list of 39morphological characteristics was compiled from previous studies (;;). The morphological characteristics of plant specimens were studied using a stereo-microscope (Olympus SZ61, Olympus, Tokyo, Japan). A digital Vernier caliper (CD-15APX, Mitutoyo, Kawasaki, Japan) was used to measure quantitative characteristics. As mentioned, all 39 morphological characters were evaluated and scored for morphological phylogenetic analysis. The characters and character states are listed in, and the data matrix is given in. Maximum parsimony analysis was carried out in TNT 1.5 (). Scores for 19 taxa were constructed, and inapplicable states were denoted as “–.” Characteristic optimization was performed in MRBAyES SLAVER 5.30 (), and cladograms of the useful characteristics were visualized using Mesquite 3.61 (). The morphological characteristics ofwas used as outgroup in the phylogenetic analysis.

Discussion

Characteristics of Barcoding Regions in

The present study investigated the possibility of classifying and examining the molecular relationships among Koreanspecies using three barcode regions (ITS2,, and). PCR amplification and sequencing of all three barcoding regions showed 100% success rate with Koreanspecies. The universality of the PCR amplification success is an important criterion for DNA barcoding (). Barcode sequence alignment analysis revealed considerable nucleotide diversity (π) between the loci, in which ITS2 showed the largest mean interspecific distance (), whereas there was no intraspecific variability among the barcode regions in 12 of the 19 taxa. In general, plastid and rDNA regions were reported as potential loci for barcoding due to the low sequence divergence (;). However, an ideal DNA barcode should be universal, reliable, cost effective, and provides considerable discriminatory power for plant species identification.

The present study showed, as single barcodes, that the species discrimination abilities of all three barcodes were poor (,), whereas the barcode combinations (ITS2 ++) improved species discrimination as well as species resolution () as reported in the previous study (). Similarly, in an earlier study,evaluated a combination of barcodes such as,,,, ITS1, and ITS2 to identify 161species. However, the present study did not include all knownspecies, as reported in previous studies (;;). There are known endemicspecies in Korea, which have a restricted distribution that needed efficient conservation strategy. Moreover, collection and conservation of manyspecies were available at the Korean gene bank. Hence, the present study was focused mainly onspecies distributed in South Korea together with available germplasm resources to preserve the biological diversity.
